title: See the Pattern
text:
Spreadsheets are great for storing data and looking up a single value. They are terrible for seeing patterns. Our eyes and brains can only hold a handful of numbers at a time, but they can take in the shape of thousands of points at a glance.
Each page on this site runs the same little experiment:

title: See the Pattern
text:
The experiments



Page
Charts
The hidden pattern is about…




Histograms & Pie Charts
histogram, pie chart
the shape of one variable and parts of a whole


Bar Charts & Boxplots
bar chart, multi-boxplot
comparing groups, and why averages can lie


Scatterplots
scatterplot
the relationship between two numeric variables


Lines Over Time
grouped line plot
trends, seasons, and sudden changes over time









NoteEvery chart shows its code



Click “Show the Python code” above any chart to see exactly how it was made with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn. The data are simulated in sim_data.py with a fixed random seed, so everyone sees the same numbers.

Your guess: For each product line, describe what’s happening over time. Growing? Shrinking? Cyclical? Did anything change suddenly?







TipReveal the grouped line plot







Show the Python code
palette = {"Outdoor gear": "#00798c", "Smart home": "#edae49", "Office supplies": "#d1495b"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
sns.lineplot(data=visits_long, x="month", y="visits", hue="product_line",
             palette=palette, marker="o", markersize=4, lw=2, ax=ax)

ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01"), color="gray", ls=":", lw=1.5)
ax.text(pd.Timestamp("2025-01-15"), ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.97, "Site redesign",
        color="gray", va="top")

ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(bymonth=[1, 7]))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b\n%Y"))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v/1000:.0f}k"))
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Monthly visits", title="Three product lines, three different stories")
ax.legend(title="", loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14), ncol=3, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Each line tells a different story, and you can read all three in seconds:

Outdoor gear is seasonal: it peaks every summer and bottoms out every winter.
Smart home is steadily growing, more than doubling over three years.
Office supplies was flat, then dropped about 40% right when the site was redesigned. That’s a problem worth investigating.

In the table, the seasonal swing looks like noise, the steady growth is spread across 36 rows, and the drop is just one column of numbers getting a bit smaller partway down.









NoteWide vs. long data





Spreadsheets usually store time series wide (one column per group). seaborn wants data long (one row per observation, with a column naming the group), which makes hue= work. Converting is one line with pandas:


Show the Python code
long = visits_wide.melt(id_vars="month", var_name="product_line", value_name="visits")

colors = sns.color_palette("Set2", len(counts))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
ax.pie(counts.values, labels=counts.index, colors=colors, autopct="%1.0f%%",
       startangle=90, counterclock=False, explode=[0.06] + [0] * (len(counts) - 1),
       wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white", "linewidth": 2}, textprops={"fontsize": 11})
ax.set_title("Nearly half of all tickets are about billing")
plt.show()









Billing alone is close to half of all tickets. In the table, “Billing” just looks like one word that comes up “a lot.”









NoteA note on pie charts





Pie charts work when you have a few categories that add up to a meaningful whole and one or two slices matter most, like here. Humans judge angles poorly, so with many similar-sized slices, a sorted bar chart is usually easier to read:


Show the Python code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(x=counts.values / counts.sum() * 100, y=counts.index, color="#2a6f97", ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Percent of tickets", ylabel="", title="Same data as a sorted bar chart")
plt.show()

title: Bar Charts & Boxplots
section: Step 1: A bar chart of averages
text:
Step 1: A bar chart of averages






TipReveal the bar chart







Show the Python code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
            hue="region", palette=palette, errorbar=None, ax=ax, legend=False)
for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt="${:,.0f}", padding=3)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Average daily sales ($)", title="Average daily sales by region")
ax.set_ylim(0, 6800)
plt.show()









The bar chart answers “which group has the biggest average?” instantly, far faster than the table. But the regions look about the same. Is that the whole story?

title: Bar Charts & Boxplots
text:
Step 2: Boxplots show the spread






TipReveal the boxplots







Show the Python code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
            hue="region", palette=palette, width=0.55, fliersize=0, ax=ax, legend=False)
sns.stripplot(data=sales, x="region", y="daily_sales", order=region_order,
              color="black", alpha=0.35, size=3.5, jitter=0.18, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Daily sales ($)",
       title="Similar averages, very different stories")
plt.show()









Now the real differences appear:

West is wildly inconsistent: some days are the best in the company, others the worst. Its average hides that.
South is actually the lowest on a normal day. Its average is propped up by 5 huge outlier days (a sale event? a data entry error?), worth investigating.
North and East are steady and predictable.

A bar chart of means compresses each group to one number. A boxplot shows the median, spread, and outliers, and overlaying the points shows every single day.









NoteThe numbers, for comparison





The same story is in the numbers if you know which ones to compute. But you need to already suspect what to look for:


Show the Python code
(sales.groupby("region")["daily_sales"]
      .agg(mean="mean", median="median", sd="std", min="min", max="max")
      .loc[region_order]
      .round(0))

title: Scatterplots
text:
Step 1: The basic scatterplot






TipReveal the scatterplot







Show the Python code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=scores, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score",
                color="#2a6f97", s=40, alpha=0.8, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score",
       title="More studying helps, but with diminishing returns")
plt.show()









Three things are visible at once:

A clear positive relationship.
It curves: the first few hours add a lot of points; hours 15–20 add very little.
A small cluster of students who studied a lot but scored poorly.

That correlation coefficient, by the way, is r = 0.68. A single number can’t tell you about the curve or the cluster.

title: Scatterplots
section: Step 2: Color by a third variable
text:
Step 2: Color by a third variable
What explains the low-scoring cluster? There’s one more column in the spreadsheet: whether the student attended the review session.






TipReveal the colored scatterplot







Show the Python code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=scores, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score", hue="attended_review",
                palette={"Yes": "#2a6f97", "No": "#d1495b"}, s=45, alpha=0.85, ax=ax)

# Smooth curve for students who attended, to show the bend
yes = scores[scores["attended_review"] == "Yes"].sort_values("hours_studied")
fit = np.polyfit(np.log1p(yes["hours_studied"]), yes["exam_score"], 1)
grid = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)
ax.plot(grid, np.polyval(fit, np.log1p(grid)), color="#2a6f97", lw=2, alpha=0.6)

ax.set(xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score",
       title="The outliers all skipped the review session")
ax.legend(title="Attended review")
plt.show()
